claims.text: Rates of major depression increased in cohorts born after World War II.
The age of onset of major depression decreased, with an increase in rates in late teenaged and early adult years.
Rates of depression increased across all age groups between 1960 and 1975.
The risk of depression is consistently two to three times higher among women than men across all adult ages.
The risk of depression is two to three times higher in first-degree relatives of affected individuals compared with controls.
The differential risk of depression between men and women is narrowing due to a greater risk increase among young men.
Increasing depression trends are evident in the United States, Sweden, Germany, Canada, and New Zealand.
Increasing depression trends are not evident in comparable studies in Korea, Puerto Rico, and Mexican-Americans living in the United States.
Cohort changes in depression rates cannot be fully attributed to artifacts of reporting, recall, mortality, or labeling.

evidence.description: Large epidemiologic and family studies suggest an increase in the rates in the cohorts born after World War II.
Studies report a decrease in the age of onset with an increase in the late teenaged and early adult years.
Epidemiologic data show an increase between 1960 and 1975 in the rates of depression for all ages.
Studies show a persistent gender effect, with the risk of depression consistently two to three times higher among women than men across all adult ages.
Family studies show a persistent family effect, with the risk about two to three times higher in first-degree relatives as compared with controls.
Data suggest a narrowing of the differential risk to men and women due to a greater increase in risk of depression among young men.
Trends drawn from studies using comparable methods and modern diagnostic criteria are evident in the United States, Sweden, Germany, Canada, and New Zealand.
Trends are not evident in comparable studies conducted in Korea and Puerto Rico and of Mexican-Americans living in the United States.
Analysis concludes cohort changes cannot be fully attributed to artifacts of reporting, recall, mortality, or labeling.

methodologies.name: Cross-national epidemiologic and family study synthesis
methodologies.description: Comparative evaluation of large epidemiologic and family cohort studies measuring temporal depression rates.

limitations.text: The reported temporal increases in depression rates are not universal and fail to appear in studies from Korea, Puerto Rico, and Mexican-Americans in the United States.
Epidemiologic cohort findings must account for potential artifacts related to reporting, recall bias, differential mortality, and changes in diagnostic labeling.

future_work.text: Investigating the specific etiology underlying secular and cohort changes in major depression rates.
Determining the implications of changing depression rates and earlier age of onset for clinical practice.
